questions.q: Is the NHS under more strain than before the pandemic?
questions.title: Is the NHS under more strain than before the pandemic?
questions.why: Four measures in four units — patients, a percentage, minutes, doctors. Small multiples give each its own scale on the same timeline, so you compare the shape and timing of each without pretending they share an axis.
questions.care: Every one of these has breaks in it: pathways dropped from the waiting list in 2013 and 2024, A&E trial sites left out from 2019 to 2023, new ambulance standards in 2017. They are marked on the lines in the explorer.
questions.sentence: The waiting list was 4.6 million in 2019 and 7.3 million in 2025, having peaked at 7.6 million in 2023. The share of A&E patients seen within four hours went from 88.0% in 2018-19 to 74.9% in 2025-26. Category 2 ambulances — strokes, heart attacks — averaged 22 minutes in 2018-19, 50 at the worst in 2022-23, and 30 in 2025-26. Fully qualified GPs have barely changed in number: 28,906 full-time equivalents in 2026, against 29,537 in 2016.
questions.description: The waiting list was 4.6 million in 2019 and 7.3 million in 2025, having peaked at 7.6 million in 2023.
questions.unit: pathways waiting · % of attendances · minutes · full-time equivalent GPs
sources: NHS England Referral to Treatment waiting times
NHS England A&E attendances and emergency admissions
NHS England General Practice Workforce statistics

questions.q: Are we living longer — and healthier?
questions.title: Are people in the UK living longer — and healthier?
questions.why: All four are in years, so they can honestly share one axis — and the space between each pair of lines is the story: the years lived in poor health.
questions.care: Period life expectancy assumes this year’s death rates hold for a whole lifetime: it summarises mortality now rather than forecasting it. Healthy life expectancy rests on people rating their own health in a survey.
questions.sentence: Life expectancy at birth rose by 3.1 years for men and 2.3 for women between 2001 and 2011, then all but stopped: by 2022 it was 79.2 for men and 83.0 for women. Healthy life expectancy — the years expected in good health — fell, from 62.7 to 60.7 for men and 63.7 to 60.9 for women. So the years a woman can expect to spend in poor health grew from 19.1 to 22.1.
questions.description: Life expectancy at birth rose by 3.1 years for men and 2.3 for women between 2001 and 2011, then all but stopped: by 2022 it was 79.2 for men and 83.0 for…

questions.q: Where does our electricity come from now?
questions.title: Where does UK electricity come from now?
questions.why: Shares of the same total over a quarter of a century. A line shows exactly when one source overtook another, which a stacked chart would bury in its middle bands.
questions.care: Low-carbon includes renewables, so those two lines overlap by design — they are not slices that add up to 100%. The space between them is nuclear.
questions.sentence: In 1998 fossil fuels made 68.5% of the UK’s electricity and renewables 2.5%. Low-carbon sources — renewables plus nuclear — overtook fossil fuels in 2017, and renewables alone did so in 2020. By 2025 renewables made 52.1% against fossil fuels’ 32.3%.
questions.description: In 1998 fossil fuels made 68.5% of the UK’s electricity and renewables 2.5%.

questions.title: Is the UK population getting older?
questions.why: The three age groups add up to the whole population, and a stacked area shows that: each band is a share of 100%. Its weakness is that only the bottom band sits on a flat baseline — the moment the over-65s overtake the under-16s is easier to see as a line, one click away in the explorer.
questions.care: These are shares, not numbers. The population grew throughout, so a smaller share of under-16s does not have to mean fewer children.
questions.sentence: In 1991 under-16s were 20.3% of the UK population and over-65s 15.8%. The over-65s overtook the under-16s in 2020, and by 2024 were 19.0% against 18.2%. The working-age share peaked at 65.1% in 2007 and is 62.8% now.
questions.description: In 1991 under-16s were 20.3% of the UK population and over-65s 15.8%. The over-65s overtook the under-16s in 2020, and by 2024 were 19.0% against 18.2%.

questions.q: Have trains, buses and cars recovered from lockdown?
questions.title: Have UK trains, buses and road traffic recovered from lockdown?
questions.why: Journeys, journeys and vehicle miles: three units at three very different sizes. Rebasing each to 100 in the same year puts them on one axis as growth, so ‘back to normal’ means the same thing for all three.
questions.care: Rail and bus figures are April-to-March years and road traffic is calendar years, so the pandemic dip lands a few months apart. Rail has several changes of method, marked in the explorer.
questions.sentence: Set each to 2010 = 100. Before the pandemic, in 2018-19, rail journeys stood at 130 and road traffic at 110, while bus journeys had fallen to 93. Lockdown took rail down to 29 and buses to 33. By 2025-26 rail was back to 135 and traffic 113, but buses only 79.
questions.description: Set each to 2010 = 100. Before the pandemic, in 2018-19, rail journeys stood at 130 and road traffic at 110, while bus journeys had fallen to 93.

questions.q: Since 2015, what has risen fastest: pay, prices, rents or house prices?
questions.title: Pay, prices, rents or house prices: what has risen fastest in the UK since 2015?
questions.why: When the question is ‘where did each one end up?’, the years in between are noise. A slope chart keeps just the start and the end, so the ranking and the size of each rise read at a glance.
questions.care: A slope chart hides the route: two series can take very different paths and finish level. Switch to a line in the explorer to see each year. The rents index starts in 2015, which is why this does too.
questions.sentence: Rebased to 2015 = 100, by 2025: pay +51%, house prices +47%, private rents +45% and prices (CPIH) +38%. Pay rose most and prices (CPIH) least.
questions.description: Rebased to 2015 = 100, by 2025: pay +51%, house prices +47%, private rents +45% and prices (CPIH) +38%. Pay rose most and prices (CPIH) least.
sources: ONS Price Index of Private Rents

questions.q: Is net migration driven by students or workers?
questions.title: Is UK net migration driven by students or workers?
questions.why: All four count people, so one axis is fair — and putting the routes beside the headline number shows which of them moved with it, and when.
questions.care: A visa granted is not a person settling: visas include short stays, study visas here exclude dependants, and net migration subtracts everyone who left. ONS changed how it estimates net migration in 2020.
questions.sentence: Net migration was 184,000 in 2019, peaked at 891,000 in 2022 and was 171,000 in 2025. Study visas peaked first, at 624,000 in 2022; work visas at 614,000 in 2023, when 348,000 health and care visas were granted. Both routes have fallen since, in step with the headline number.
questions.description: Net migration was 184,000 in 2019, peaked at 891,000 in 2022 and was 171,000 in 2025.
sources: Home Office entry clearance visa statistics

questions.title: Are children in England getting heavier?
questions.why: Each dot is one school year’s measurement. Dots rather than a line make plain that this is a yearly check, and stop one odd year from dragging a line up and down with it.
questions.care: England only. The 2020/21 figures come from a much smaller sample of schools measured during the pandemic, so that year’s jump should be read with care.
questions.sentence: Obesity among reception children was 9.9% in 2006/07 and 10.5% in 2024/25 — little changed. Among Year 6 children it went from 17.5% to 22.2%. Children now leave primary school about 2.1 times as likely to be obese as when they start it.
questions.description: Obesity among reception children was 9.9% in 2006/07 and 10.5% in 2024/25 — little changed. Among Year 6 children it went from 17.5% to 22.2%.

questions.q: Are we building as many homes as we used to?
questions.title: Is England building as many homes as it used to?
questions.why: Homes completed is a count for each year, so each column is one year’s output and its height the total. Columns make the size of the post-war peak against today plain in a way a thin line does not.
questions.care: These are completions counted by councils and building control in England. They miss conversions and changes of use, which the ‘net additions’ measure includes, so they understate how many homes the stock gains.
questions.sentence: England completed 353,000 new homes in 1968, the most in any year since the war. In the last thirty years the most in a single year was 178,000, in 2022, and in 2025 it was 142,000 — 40% of the 1968 peak.
questions.description: England completed 353,000 new homes in 1968, the most in any year since the war.

questions.q: When did the government last balance the books?
questions.title: When did the UK government last balance the books?
questions.why: Borrowing is one total per year and can go below zero when there is a surplus. Columns above and below the line show each year’s sign at a glance — and as a share of GDP, 1950 and 2020 compare fairly.
questions.care: In cash terms every recent year would dwarf the past, which is why this is a share of the economy. A surplus here is the whole public sector’s, before any one-off transfers are taken out.
questions.sentence: The government borrowed in 65 of the 78 years from 1948 to 2025. The last surplus was in 2001. Borrowing peaked at 12.7% of GDP in 2020; in 2025 it was 5.0%.
questions.description: The government borrowed in 65 of the 78 years from 1948 to 2025. The last surplus was in 2001. Borrowing peaked at 12.7% of GDP in 2020; in 2025 it was 5.0%.

questions.q: Are deaths about to overtake births?
questions.title: Are deaths about to overtake births in England and Wales?
questions.why: The question is about the difference between two lines. A gap chart shades it, so you read births minus deaths — the natural change in the population — directly, and see how close the lines have come.
questions.care: England and Wales only. With the gap this narrow, population growth now comes almost entirely from migration.
questions.sentence: In 1947 births outnumbered deaths in England and Wales by 363,000. In 2025 the gap was 14,000: 585,000 births against 571,000 deaths. Deaths last outnumbered births in 1977, one of only two years since 1938 when they did.
questions.description: In 1947 births outnumbered deaths in England and Wales by 363,000. In 2025 the gap was 14,000: 585,000 births against 571,000 deaths.
sources: ONS Births in England and Wales
ONS Deaths registered in England and Wales

questions.title: Did UK productivity stop growing after 2008?
questions.why: One series over half a century. A line shows the change of slope — the bend at 2008 — and the bend is the whole story.
questions.care: Productivity is output per hour worked across the whole economy. It is hard to measure and is revised often, so the last year or two may move.
questions.sentence: Output per hour grew by 2.2% a year on average from 1971 to 2007, and 0.4% a year from 2007 to 2025. Had the old rate carried on, the index would be about 138 today rather than 99 — roughly 39% higher.
questions.description: Output per hour grew by 2.2% a year on average from 1971 to 2007, and 0.4% a year from 2007 to 2025.

questions.title: Has crime gone up in England and Wales?
questions.why: Two measures of the same thing at very different sizes. Rebasing both to 100 shows the direction of each, and the year they part ways.
questions.care: Police figures rose from 2014 largely because recording was tightened after inspectors found crimes going unrecorded. The survey misses crimes against businesses, only counts fraud from 2016, and paused in 2020.
questions.sentence: Police-recorded crime has risen 49% since its low in 2013-14 — the rise most headlines report. The Crime Survey, which asks people what happened to them and does not depend on what the police record, shows crime down 65% since 2002-03, and 78% lower than its peak in 1995-96.
questions.description: Police-recorded crime has risen 49% since its low in 2013-14 — the rise most headlines report.
sources: ONS Crime in England and Wales
ONS Crime in England and Wales (Home Office police recorded crime)

questions.title: Is Britain getting unhappier?
questions.why: The scale runs from 0 to 10, so the axis does too. Zoom in to fit the data — as most charts, and the explorer by default, do — and a quarter-point wobble fills the frame.
questions.care: These are averages of a very large survey, so a tenth of a point is a real change across the population, even if no one person would notice it. Lower is better for anxiety.
questions.sentence: On a scale of 0 to 10, average happiness moved between 7.29 and 7.56 over 12 years — 0.27 of a point. The biggest move came in the pandemic: anxiety rose from 2.87 in 2018-19 to 3.31 in 2020-21, and was 3.23 in 2022-23. Drawn from zero, as here, the lines are close to flat. Cut the axis to fit the data and the same numbers look like a collapse.
questions.description: On a scale of 0 to 10, average happiness moved between 7.29 and 7.56 over 12 years — 0.27 of a point.

questions.q: Are more people dying than ever?
questions.title: Are more people dying than ever in England and Wales?
questions.why: The axis starts at zero, which shows a flat line for what it is. Why it is flat is the surprise: far more people, each living far longer.
questions.care: These are deaths registered in the year, which can lag the death itself — most of all when a coroner is involved.
questions.sentence: Deaths in England and Wales have stayed between 445,000 (1923) and 612,000 (1918) every year since 1900. In 2025 there were 571,000. Since 1971 the UK population has grown by 24%, yet deaths in 2025 were within 1% of the 567,000 in 1971.
questions.description: Deaths in England and Wales have stayed between 445,000 (1923) and 612,000 (1918) every year since 1900. In 2025 there were 571,000.
sources: ONS Deaths registered in England and Wales

questions.title: Has Britain stopped saving?
questions.why: A dashed line at the long-run average turns ‘is it low?’ into something you can see: the ratio crosses it again and again, which is what no trend looks like.
questions.care: The saving ratio is what is left of disposable income after spending, so it falls when spending rises as well as when income falls. It is revised heavily, often years later.
questions.sentence: Households have saved between 5.1% (2022) and 16.6% (2020) of their disposable income since 1963, 9.4% on average. In 2025 it was 9.7%, close to that average. The highs line up with recessions and the 2020 lockdown, when spending fell — there is no long slide.
questions.description: Households have saved between 5.1% (2022) and 16.6% (2020) of their disposable income since 1963, 9.4% on average. In 2025 it was 9.7%, close to that average.

questions.q: Did Brexit tip Britain into a trade deficit?
questions.title: Did Brexit tip Britain into a trade deficit?
questions.why: A balance can sit either side of zero. Columns above and below the line show each year’s surplus or deficit, and as a share of GDP 1950 and 2020 compare fairly.
questions.care: This is goods and services together: a long-standing deficit in goods is partly offset by a surplus in services. Trade figures are revised often, and trade in precious metals can swing a single year.
questions.sentence: The UK ran a trade deficit in every one of the 18 years from 1998 to 2015, before the referendum, and in nine of the 10 years since. It averaged 1.5% of GDP a year before the vote and 0.8% after. The deficit is decades old.
questions.description: The UK ran a trade deficit in every one of the 18 years from 1998 to 2015, before the referendum, and in nine of the 10 years since.

questions.q: Do more police officers mean more crimes charged?
questions.title: Do more police officers mean more crimes charged?
questions.why: Each dot is a year, placed by officer numbers across and charge rate up. If more officers meant more charges the dots would climb to the right. Joining them in time order shows what is really going on.
questions.care: A scatter of yearly totals cannot show cause either way. Charge rates also depend on how crimes are recorded and what kinds are reported, and both changed over these years. Officers are counted at March, charge rates by financial year.
questions.sentence: Across these 12 years, if anything the years with more officers had lower charge rates (a correlation of −0.41). Officer numbers fell to 122,000 in 2018 and rose to 148,000 by 2024; the charge rate fell from 15.5% to 5.6% in 2021-22, and is back to 8.5%. Both moved with time, for their own reasons — the dots trace a loop, not a line.
questions.description: Across these 12 years, if anything the years with more officers had lower charge rates (a correlation of −0.41).
sources: Home Office Police workforce, England and Wales
Home Office Crime Outcomes in England and Wales
